data.title: Domain Registration Exposes Named Staff and Contact Routes
data.summary:
Domain registration records disclose named individuals, direct telephone numbers and
role-based addresses, supplying both targets for pretexting and the means to attempt
domain control.
data.description:
Registration records are a small but high-quality source. The named contact is usually a
real person with genuine authority over the domain, which makes them a precise target for
a pretext aimed at transfer or DNS change — the highest-impact outcome available from
social engineering against an organisation's internet presence.

Historical records compound the problem. Privacy protection applied later does not remove
what was published before, and archived records remain retrievable.

Inconsistent protection across a portfolio is the common pattern: the main domain is
protected while older or peripheral registrations are not, and those are frequently the
ones with weaker account security as well.
data.recommendation:
* Apply registrar privacy consistently across the whole domain portfolio, not only the
  primary domains.
* Use role-based addresses on a monitored mailbox rather than named individuals.
* Enable registrar and registry transfer locks, and require multi-factor authentication on
  registrar accounts.
* Treat historical records as already disclosed and brief the named individuals accordingly.
data.short_recommendation: Apply registrar privacy portfolio-wide and enable transfer locks.
